clinicalPearls: A mixed syndrome in which a pericardial effusion coexists with constriction from an inflamed, non-compliant visceral pericardium
The defining feature is that right atrial pressure fails to fall appreciably after the effusion is drained, unmasking underlying constriction
Presents with features of both tamponade and constriction, including raised jugular venous pressure, breathlessness, and signs of systemic venous congestion
Causes overlap with those of pericarditis and constriction, including idiopathic and viral disease, tuberculosis, malignancy, radiation, and prior cardiac surgery
Diagnosis classically requires haemodynamic assessment before and after pericardiocentesis, though echocardiography and cross-sectional imaging increasingly support recognition
Some cases resolve as the pericardial inflammation settles, so a trial of anti-inflammatory therapy may be appropriate when active inflammation is present
Persistent constriction after drainage may ultimately require pericardiectomy, which typically means removing the constricting visceral layer
reference.pathophysiology: In effusive-constrictive pericarditis two processes coexist: fluid accumulates within the pericardial space while the visceral pericardium becomes inflamed, thickened, and rigid. Removing the fluid relieves the tamponade component but not the constraint imposed by the stiff visceral layer, so ventricular filling remains impaired and right atrial pressure stays elevated after drainage, which is the haemodynamic hallmark. The constriction reflects the same fibro-inflammatory response seen in constrictive pericarditis and may be transient if the inflammation resolves, or may become established and fixed, mirroring the aetiologies of pericarditis and constriction more generally.
additionalDifferentials: Severe tricuspid regurgitation with right heart failure
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to demonstrate effusion, septal bounce, respiratory variation, and impaired filling
Right heart catheterisation with pressure measurement before and after pericardiocentesis
Cardiac CT and MRI to assess pericardial thickening, inflammation, and calcification
Analysis of pericardial fluid for infection, tuberculosis, and malignancy when the cause is unclear
Inflammatory markers to gauge activity and the likelihood of response to anti-inflammatory therapy
redFlags: Persistent raised right atrial pressure and low output after apparently adequate pericardiocentesis
Haemodynamic collapse suggesting the tamponade component predominates
Features of tuberculous or malignant pericardial disease
Progressive constriction with worsening right heart failure despite treatment
reference.prognosis: The outlook depends on the cause; inflammation-related cases may be transient and resolve with medical therapy, whereas established constriction after drainage often requires pericardiectomy and carries the risks of that operation.
pitfalls: Assuming pericardiocentesis alone will resolve symptoms and overlooking persistent constriction
Failing to measure right atrial pressure before and after drainage to reveal the constrictive component
Missing tuberculous or malignant aetiology that alters management and prognosis
Proceeding to early pericardiectomy in cases that would settle with anti-inflammatory treatment
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases
management: Relieve the tamponade component with pericardiocentesis, recognising that constriction persists as right atrial pressure fails to normalise after drainage
Treat active pericardial inflammation with anti-inflammatory therapy using NSAIDs and colchicine, with corticosteroids in selected cases, as some cases are transient and resolve
Treat the underlying cause directly, with antituberculous therapy for tuberculous disease and management of malignancy, uraemia or radiation-related pericarditis
Offer pericardiectomy with removal of the visceral and parietal layers for established, symptomatic constriction that does not resolve with medical therapy
Manage congestive symptoms with cautious diuresis while avoiding excessive preload reduction
Monitor with serial echocardiography, cross-sectional imaging and inflammatory markers to judge resolution versus fixed constriction
Manage through cardiology with cardiac surgery referral for pericardiectomy
